newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDIC finds lending standards generally sound.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDIC finds lending standards generally sound.

text.p: U.S. bank underwriting standards are generally sound but some institutions are engaging in lending practices that could lead to future problems, a leading regulator said Wednesday.

"We are pleased by the stability of credit underwriting standards at banks we've examined since early 1995, but there are some probems that deserve closer monitoring," Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Chairman Ricki Helfer said in a statement accompanying the survey.

The latest FDIC survey covered lending practices during the six months ending March 31, 1997, at 1,277 state-chartered banks and savings institutions for which the FDIC was the primary federal regulator.

Some 91 percent of these banks had no material change in underwriting practices since the previous examination, six percent were judged to have tightened lending practices and three percent loosened their standards.
FDIC examiners cited the following areas of potential concern:
-- Thirteen percent of the institutions were judged to have "above-average" risk in their loan administration,
-- Approximately six percent of the banks had high concentrations of loans to one borrower or industry,
-- Twenty-two percent of 593 active construction lenders customarily funded speculative projects,
-- and seven percent of the 619 banks active in agricultural lending had portfolios tied to major crops affected by the phaseout of farm susidies enacted by Congress last year.
